frames.narration: The wrong way first: the database password is written in the source code. It is now in every clone, every backup and the full Git history, and anyone with read access to the repository has it.
The better way: the application contains no secret. When it starts, it proves who it is to the secrets manager, using its platform identity (a cloud role or service account).

messages.label: I am payments-service, here is my identity

frames.narration: The secrets manager checks that this identity may read this secret, and writes the access to an audit log.
Even better, it asks the database to create a new account just for this service, valid for one hour.
The application receives that short-lived credential and uses it. It never wrote it to disk or to a log.
Suppose that credential leaks. It expires within the hour, it only works for this one account, and the audit log shows exactly when it was issued and to whom.

For a long-lived secret such as a third-party API key, the manager rotates it on a schedule, and the application reloads the new value without a redeploy. Rotating is routine, so a real leak is a normal task.
